blocks.text: The Knocking Beneath the Current
Era Three · Spooky mystery · A healer's record
Low water: arrival
The first entry in the refuge book was practical.
Breathing exchange cleared. Two clean wraps. Four sealed food jars. Hinged probe missing.
The second was in another hand.
If somebody knocks from the river, make certain your companion is still beside you.

I was the new river healer. I disliked this sort of warning. It made no distinction between an old joke and a useful instruction, and it occupied space where somebody might have described the missing probe.
Suth watched me read it. They were unrolling a sleeping mat beneath the curved ceiling, which at low water showed stones and a long root braided around the outside glass.
“Would you cross it out?” they asked.
“I would ask whoever wrote it to explain.”
“They're gone.”

That was how Suth spoke of Renn. Gone could mean a journey, a death, a refusal to return, or a route no longer available. I had not asked which. Suth had shown me where the hatch appeared, how to lower its stone lid, and how to test the exchange that kept the room habitable under the current. They were entitled to a few unanswered questions.

Our room occupied a side channel that local boat people counted as part of the River of Deferred Reflections. Others said the true river ran beyond the next reed bank. Our water had enough wrong images to make the distinction academic.
That afternoon a bridge appeared overhead. There had been no bridge there when we entered. Something with long jointed legs crossed its reflection, stopped, and bent toward the water.
Suth pulled a cloth across the viewing strip.
“We don't know whether that one wanted to be seen,” they said.
We ate by the little maintenance light.
Rising water: three knocks
The knocks came after Suth slept.
Three. A pause. Two.
Not loud. I first thought a stone had rolled across the roof. Then came three again, from the far wall, beneath the point where the old migration map had peeled away.
“Suth?”
They woke immediately.
I had not heard anyone wake so quickly before.
The knocking stopped.
“Branches,” Suth said.
There were no branches on that side of the room. I knew because I had cleared the bank myself.
We listened until the exchange clicked through its next cycle. Its click was followed by a weak, dragging breath. I wrote that down.
In the morning, a figure stood in the water above us.
The current went through it. Its outline was narrow, its head tilted as if listening beneath the surface. One forelimb was wrapped in pale cloth.
Suth set down their bowl so carefully that I heard each edge meet the floor.
“Renn,” they said.
The figure did not turn.
The old water continued uphill through its shoulder. A long-bodied fish passed through the pale bandage and cast an entirely ordinary shadow on our ceiling.
“An image,” I said.
“I know what an image is.”
Suth had helped paint Renn's boat. They had shown Renn how to brace the wrapped forelimb. They could identify a beloved person without believing that every likeness was that person returned.
I wished I had said something else.
High water: the wrong bank

The refuge should have been safe through the flood. That was why we were there. Three families upstream knew they could descend at the next low interval if the reed shelters failed. I needed to learn the room before I was responsible for frightened children inside it.
By the second evening the exchange was clicking too often.

I opened its inner grille. Fine sediment had gathered behind it in a crescent, too deep for my fingers. The missing hinged probe would have reached the outside bend. The straight one reached nothing useful.
Suth knelt beside me.
“Renn made the other tool.”
“Where is it?”
“I don't know.”
They had folded their hands so tightly that the small joints had gone pale.
Above us, the reflected Renn knelt too.
I looked away, then looked back. The image had its bandaged limb against a stone at the edge of an old bank. It lifted the stone. Something bright lay underneath.
Suth made a short sound. Hope can sound remarkably like someone being hurt.
“It was there,” they said. “The tool. On the east bank.”

The present east bank was underwater. The image might be from another season or another generation; it might show a repair repeated a hundred times. Nothing in it could tell us where the tool was now.
At that moment the knocks sounded again.
Three. A pause. Two.
Suth answered against the wall.
I caught their hand before the second sequence.
“Tell me.”
For a long time they would not look at me.
Then they said, “Renn used that when a hatch was stuck. Three to say they were outside. Two to ask whether I was awake.”
“When did they leave?”
“Before the last long flood. We quarreled. I said they cared more about the river than anyone waiting at home. They took the downstream boat.”
“Did anyone see it arrive?”
“No.”
The word remained between us. It did not become death because I was a healer, or survival because Suth wanted it to.
We did not open the hatch.
High water: experiment
I put a bowl of water beside the exchange and waited for the knocks.
At each knock a small ring moved across the bowl. The reflected Renn remained still. When the image lifted its arm, nothing disturbed the surface.
I asked Suth to move the inner baffle through a half turn. The exchange clicked. The knocking stopped halfway through its sequence.
I should have been pleased. Instead I felt ashamed of the pleasure I had expected. I had wanted a simple mechanism to excuse me from standing beside Suth's uncertainty.
We repeated the test. The baffle controlled the sound. It did not control the figure.

Something solid was tapping in the outer exchange. Water pressure carried the noise around the wall. That explained the changing direction. It did not explain why the pattern repeated so neatly, or why it had begun now.
We could survive until the next low water if we reduced our activity and cleared the inner sediment. We could not shelter three families with the exchange like this.
“I have to go out when the current falls,” I said.
Suth nodded.
“And you have to guide me. The present bank, Suth. I need the present bank.”
They took down the migration map. Under it were older hand-drawn maps, none quite aligned. They chose a blank corner and began drawing what we had actually seen that morning.
Falling water: the tool
The current thinned enough to expose the hatch before it exposed the bank. I tied a line around my middle and pushed into water the color of old leaves.
Suth remained at the hatch, braced against its rim. They could see my line. They could not see my face.
The old reflected bank crossed the real one at a slant. I nearly put my weight on its convincing stone. Suth pulled once, hard. My foot entered empty water where the image had promised a ledge.
“Left,” they said. “The root is yours. The stone isn't.”
I reached the exchange by crawling along the root.
Something tapped my fingers from inside the grille.
Three times.
I nearly let go.

The hinged probe was lodged across the opening. Its loose handle rose with the pressure, struck the grille, settled, and rose again. Silt had packed around its bend. I worked the handle sideways, scraped a channel with my smallest claw, and felt the packed mud begin to loosen.
It came free with a rush that pulled me face-first toward the opening.
Suth's line caught me. The knot hurt. I have seldom loved a knot more.
When they hauled me to the hatch, I was holding the tool so fiercely that they had to unfold my fingers.
Renn's repair mark was on the handle.
Neither of us said it meant Renn had been there recently. Neither of us said it did not.
Low water: departure
We brought the upstream families through the hatch that evening. A child asked why the ceiling contained someone standing where there was no ground.
“Old light,” Suth said. “We don't have to watch it.”
The child asked whether old light could see them.
“I don't know,” Suth answered, then considered. “We have no reason to think so.”
They hung the cloth. The child immediately became more interested in a food jar.
We wrote a proper repair note. We drew the exchange, the baffle, the bend that collected sediment. We recorded the probe's recovery and tied it beside the grille.
Suth also wrote a message for boat people: RENN, IF THIS REACHES YOU, THE LOWER REFUGE IS OPEN. I WILL RECEIVE AN ANSWER. YOU NEED NOT RETURN TO GIVE ONE.
I offered to add Suth's home route. They declined. The refuge was enough.

Before we left, I returned to the warning in the book. I did not cross it out. Beneath it I wrote: Sound may travel through the breathing exchange. Test pressure before opening anything. A reflection cannot verify a visitor.
Suth read that and added: Keep listening for living people anyway.
We climbed out together. The last family followed. I counted every head while Suth lowered the lid.
From the dry chamber beneath us came two knocks.
The tool was in my bag; we were taking it to be straightened. The exchange was running freely. I had counted everybody.
Suth looked at me.
We waited, then lifted the hatch and called into the room. No one answered. We inspected the benches, the grille, the little store recess. We found nobody left behind.
I entered all of this in the book.
I did not enter branches.
